blocks.text: A learning rate scheduler determines how the learning rate changes over the course of training, rather than staying fixed at one value the entire time, typically starting higher and gradually decreasing, working together with the warmup technique covered in the previous topic of this module.
This topic covers the most common scheduling shapes, linear and cosine decay, and how to choose and monitor a schedule for a fine-tuning run.
1. What a Learning Rate Scheduler Does

blocks.alt: A training step feeds into the scheduler, producing the learning rate at that step

blocks.text: Rather than using one fixed learning rate value for every single training step, a scheduler computes a different learning rate depending on how far into training the current step is, following a predetermined pattern chosen ahead of time.
2. Constant vs Scheduled Learning Rate

blocks.alt: A constant learning rate is compared against a scheduled one

blocks.text: A constant learning rate is the simplest choice, one fixed value throughout training, but a scheduled learning rate, typically starting higher and decreasing over time, often produces better final results, since a higher rate early on helps training progress quickly while a lower rate later helps the model settle more precisely into a good solution.
3. Linear Decay

blocks.alt: A high learning rate at the start decreases steadily and linearly down to a low value at the end

blocks.text: Linear decay reduces the learning rate by the same fixed amount at each step, tracing a straight line from its starting value down to its final value over the course of training, a simple, predictable schedule shape.

code.content:
# A simple linear decay schedule
def linear_decay_lr(step, total_steps, start_lr, end_lr):
    progress = step / total_steps
    return start_lr + (end_lr - start_lr) * progress

blocks.text: 4. Cosine Decay

blocks.alt: A high learning rate at the start decreases along a smooth curved shape down to a low value at the end

blocks.text: Cosine decay follows a smooth, curved shape based on the cosine mathematical function, decreasing slowly at first, more quickly through the middle of training, and slowly again near the end, a pattern many practitioners have found works particularly well for fine-tuning and is one of the most commonly used schedule shapes today.

blocks.text: 5. Combining Warmup With a Decay Schedule

blocks.alt: A warmup phase leads into a decay phase, forming the complete schedule

blocks.text: In practice, warmup and decay are almost always combined into one complete schedule, the learning rate ramps up during the warmup phase covered in the previous topic, reaches its peak target value, and then follows a decay shape, linear or cosine, for the remainder of training.

blocks.title: This full shape is the standard pattern across most fine-tuning setups
blocks.content: A warmup followed by cosine decay is one of the most widely used complete learning rate schedules in modern fine-tuning, appearing as a common default across many training frameworks covered in the Fine-Tuning Frameworks module later in this course.

blocks.text: 6. Step Based vs Epoch Based Scheduling

blocks.alt: Updates happening every step are compared against updates happening every epoch

blocks.text: A scheduler can update the learning rate after every single training step, giving fine grained control, or only after every full epoch, a coarser update pattern, with step based scheduling being the more common choice for fine-tuning, since it allows the learning rate to change smoothly throughout even a single epoch of training.
7. Choosing a Scheduler for Fine-Tuning

For most fine-tuning projects, a warmup period followed by cosine decay, covered above, is a reasonable, well tested default, and experimenting with alternative schedule shapes is usually only worth the effort once basic training is working well and finer tuning is being explored.
8. Monitoring Whether a Schedule Is Working

blocks.alt: The loss curve gets checked for whether the schedule is working well, then kept or adjusted

blocks.text: The same loss curve monitoring covered in the earlier SFT Training Pipeline topic doubles as a way to judge whether a chosen schedule is working well, a smoothly decreasing loss curve that flattens out gently near the end of training is generally a good sign, while a curve that plateaus too early or remains noisy throughout may indicate the schedule needs adjustment.
9. Scheduler Interactions With Other Hyperparameters

The schedule shape interacts with total training length, batch size, and the base learning rate itself, changing any one of these often means the others, including the schedule, need to be reconsidered together rather than adjusted in complete isolation, similar to the paired relationship between rank and alpha covered in the LoRA module.
Worked Example

A team fine-tuning for three epochs uses a schedule combining a short warmup covering the first five percent of steps with cosine decay for the remainder, watching their loss curve rise briefly during warmup before settling into a smooth, steady decrease that flattens gently by the final epoch.

When they experiment with a constant learning rate instead, keeping everything else the same, they observe a noisier loss curve that does not settle as cleanly near the end of training, confirming the value the scheduled approach provided for their specific setup.
Common Mistakes

items: Using a constant learning rate by default without considering whether a scheduled approach would improve final results
Choosing a decay schedule without pairing it with warmup, missing the stability benefit covered in the previous topic
Changing batch size or total training length without reconsidering whether the existing schedule still makes sense
Not monitoring the loss curve to judge whether a chosen schedule is actually behaving as intended

blocks.text: Practice

For a training run of your choosing, sketch what a warmup plus cosine decay schedule would look like over the full course of training, marking roughly where the peak learning rate occurs and how it decreases afterward.
Key Takeaway

A learning rate scheduler changes the learning rate over the course of training rather than keeping it fixed, with warmup followed by cosine decay serving as a well tested default for most fine-tuning projects, and monitoring the resulting loss curve is the most direct way to judge whether a chosen schedule is genuinely working well for a specific training run.
